y-m-79-01.title: The same box plot, different means?
y-m-79-01.topic: Quartiles and interpreting a box plot
y-m-79-01.goal: From a five-number summary (minimum, quartiles, median, maximum), separate what can and cannot be said for certain, and make different data sets yourself that share the same summary to show the limits of the summary.
y-m-79-01.material:
The teacher gave the results of a performance assessment (0 to 50 points, all scores integers) taken by 7 students in one class only as a 'five-number summary'.

Minimum 10 points, first quartile 15 points, median 20 points, third quartile 30 points, maximum 50 points.

Convention: if the scores of the 7 students arranged from smallest to largest are x1, x2, ..., x7 (x-one through x-seven), the minimum is x1, the first quartile is x2, the median is x4, the third quartile is x6, and the maximum is x7. Several students may have the same score.
y-m-79-01.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-79-01.thinking.1: Making different data sets with the same summary (counterexamples)
y-m-79-01.thinking.2: Stating the limits of comparing with box plots
y-m-79-01.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: how to arrange data from smallest to largest and find the median and quartiles, and the meaning of the mean. In this task, it is agreed that the quartiles of 7 data values are the '2nd, 4th, and 6th values from smallest' (the way of determining quartiles may differ slightly from textbook to textbook).
y-m-79-01.s.s1.prompt: Knowing only this summary, choose everything that can be said to be definitely true.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.hint.0: Draw 7 boxes for x1 to x7, and first write in the scores for the boxes the summary tells you.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.hint.1: Find which box the student in each choice refers to, and check whether that box's score is determined or empty.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.o.a: The average score of the students in this class is 20 points.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.a: The mean is not in the summary. The median and the mean are different values, and reading the middle value as the mean would assume all scores in this class are around 20.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.o.b: The student who is 4th from the smallest has 20 points.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.b: In this convention the median is the 4th value. You read exactly the position that the summary tells you.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.o.c: Exactly two students have 30 points or more.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.c: Even if x6 is 30 points, that doesn't settle that x5 is less than 30. The 5th student may also have 30 points, so you can't say 'exactly'.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.o.d: At least 4 students have 20 points or more.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.d: If x4 is 20 points, then x5, x6, and x7 cannot be smaller than x4. You used the order to get 'at least'.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.r.e: x3 or x5 may also be 20 points. If you think a value in the summary appears only once, you miss the possibility that there are more students with the same score.
y-m-79-01.s.s1.explain: There are 7 students, so the 4th from the smallest is the median, 20 points, and the 4th to 7th students all have 20 points or more, so 'at least 4' is certain. On the other hand, for x3 we know only that it is 15 or more and 20 or less, and for x5 only that it is 20 or more and 30 or less, and we don't know exact values. So the mean, 'exactly how many have 30 or more', and 'exactly how many have 20' are not settled by this summary alone.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 2 sets of scores that share the same summary (x1=10, x2=15, x4=20, x6=30, x7=50) but have different means. Enter the 7 scores in order from smallest.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.hint.0: First fill in the boxes x1, x2, x4, x6, x7 as in the summary, and find which two boxes are empty.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.hint.1: Decide the range of values that can go in the two empty boxes by comparing them with the scores of the boxes on either side.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.hint.2: Add up all the scores of both data sets and check that the means actually differ.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.ok.c1: They are arranged from smallest to largest.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.fail.c1: The scores are not in order from smallest. An earlier value cannot be greater than a later value.
y-m-79-01.s.s2.fail.c2: x1, x2, x4, x6, x7 differ from the summary (10, 15, 20, 30, 50).
y-m-79-01.s.s2.explain: x3 can be chosen between 15 and 20 points, and x5 between 20 and 30 points. For example, (10, 15, 15, 20, 20, 30, 50) has a mean of about 22.9 points, and (10, 15, 20, 20, 30, 30, 50) has a mean of 25 points. The summary is the same but the means differ.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.prompt: If two data sets draw the same box plot but have different means, what would you like to tell someone who tries to 'compare the means' by looking only at the box plots of two classes? You may use the numbers of the data you made.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.hint.0: Write the mean of each of the two data sets you made above.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.hint.1: Write down separately one piece of information a box plot holds and one it does not.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The means of the two data sets are about 22.9 points and 25 points, so ...
y-m-79-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you cite the mean (or the total) of the two data sets you made as your evidence?
y-m-79-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you make clear that 'the box plots are the same' and 'the means are the same' are different statements?
y-m-79-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also say what a box plot can tell you (for example, the median and where the spread lies)?
y-m-79-01.s.s3.model.0: The two data sets have the same minimum, quartiles, median, and maximum, but the means were different, about 22.9 points and 25 points. So even if the box plots are the same, the means can differ, and you must not compare means using box plots alone. The median and the spread can be compared.
y-m-79-01.s.s3.model.1: Even if only the 3rd and 5th students' scores change, the mean changes while the five-number summary stays the same. The mean is not determined by the summary values alone, so I'd like to say that if you are curious about the mean, you have to know the original scores.

y-m-79-02.title: Which of the two practice methods is more effective?
y-m-79-02.topic: Comparing by strata and Simpson's paradox
y-m-79-02.goal: Confirm with data that the overall proportion and the group proportions can point in opposite directions, and judge which comparison is more trustworthy and what other information is needed.
y-m-79-02.material: 700 members of a running club practiced with one of two practice methods for one month, and a survey asked whether they achieved their personal target time. The members chose the practice method themselves, and also chose their practice course, either an 'easy course' or a 'hard course'. 350 people chose method A and 350 people chose method B. (Achievement rate = number who achieved ÷ number of people in that group)
y-m-79-02.thinking.0: Revising or keeping your judgment as data grows
y-m-79-02.thinking.2: Judging whether the comparison is fair
y-m-79-02.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: calculating and comparing ratios (percentages), and comparing two groups with the same total. No mathematical probability formulas are needed.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.prompt: One piece of data is revealed at each step. Each time, choose your judgment for now. You do not have to change your earlier judgment.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.hint.0: Divide the number who achieved in each method and course by the total number in that cell, write it in a table, and compare the two methods on the same line.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.hint.1: Write side by side how many people in each method are in the easy course and the hard course, and look at which rate the overall rate is closer to.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.info: Overall results: for method A, 273 of 350 achieved the target, and for method B, 289 of 350 achieved it.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.ask: With the data so far, which practice method do you think is more effective?
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.after: The overall achievement rate is about 78.0% for A and about 82.6% for B. Reading it as B being higher is reasonable, and holding off because the members chose for themselves is also reasonable.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A is more effective. The numbers of people are the same, so the people on A's side did better.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.a: More people achieved with B. Compare the numbers again to see which is higher.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.b: B seems more effective. Out of the same 350 people, more achieved.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You read the numbers accurately. However, you can check further in the next step whether this is the 'effect of the method'.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.c: I won't decide yet. The members chose the methods themselves, so I need to know more about what kind of people chose.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You first thought that the characteristics of the people who chose can get mixed into the result.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The two methods are the same. The numbers who achieved are similar, 273 and 289.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.0.r.d: A difference of 16 people is too early to call the same. First express it as a rate and check how much it differs.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.info: Results by course: in the easy course, 81 of 87 people (about 93.1%) achieved with A, and 234 of 270 (about 86.7%) with B. In the hard course, 192 of 263 people (about 73.0%) achieved with A, and 55 of 80 (about 68.8%) with B.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.ask: Now which practice method do you think is more effective?
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.after: In both the easy course and the hard course, A's achievement rate is higher. But the overall is higher for B, so it is possible to guess that the makeup of courses differs greatly from method to method.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The calculation must be wrong. If A is higher in both courses, B can't be higher overall.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.a: If you recalculate the totals and rates yourself, all are correct. This can really happen when the sizes of the groups are different.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.b: I keep my first judgment that B is better. It was higher overall and the numbers of people are the same, so the overall comparison is the fairest.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.b: We have not yet checked whether the makeup of courses is the same for the two methods. Having the same total number of people does not mean the makeup is the same.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.c: My judgment leans toward A. Comparing within the same course, A is higher in both courses.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You thought of comparing under the same conditions. However, why the overall result is the opposite is something to check in the next step.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.o.d: I won't decide. Within the same course A is higher, but I need to first look at the makeup of the people who chose each course for each method.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is a judgment that wants to check the makeup first when the results conflict. The information in the next step is exactly that makeup.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.info: Makeup of course choices: of the 350 who chose method A, 263 (about 75.1%) chose the hard course, and of the 350 who chose method B, 270 (about 77.1%) chose the easy course. With either method, the easy course had a higher achievement rate.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.ask: Which comparison is more trustworthy for comparing the effect of the methods?
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.after: Comparing by course reduces the influence of difficulty, but the fact that the members chose the practice method themselves remains. If people with greater ability chose a particular method, it mixes with the effect of the method. So saying together 'the comparison by course is more trustworthy' and 'it is still hard to be sure' is also fitting.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.a: The overall comparison is more trustworthy. Both groups are 350 people, so it is fair.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.a: Having the same number of people does not mean the makeup of course difficulty is the same. A was concentrated in the hard course.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.b: I look only at the hard course. The result from the course where more people gathered (263 and 80) is more trustworthy.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.b: In the hard course, B has only 80 people. If you use only one course, you throw away the information from the other course.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.c: The comparison by course is better. Difficulty affects achievement, so compare within the same difficulty.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You compared in a way that filters out the influence of difficulty. However, the reason for choosing the course (for example, ability) still remains.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.o.d: It is hard to settle on either. The comparison by course is better, but the members chose the method themselves, so differences in ability may remain.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You thought even about the limits of observational data. It links to why a design that divides people at random is needed.
y-m-79-02.s.s1.reflect: How did your judgment differ between step 1 and step 3? The overall rate seemed convincing at first, so what information made that comparison hard to trust? If you kept your first judgment, what further grounds did you add?
y-m-79-02.s.s2.prompt: The club wants to check the effect of the practice methods in a more trustworthy way. Which approach is most fitting?
y-m-79-02.s.s2.hint.0: Compare who decides 'who uses each method, on which course'.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.hint.1: Write one reason why a lopsided makeup arises for each method, and mark the approach that can remove that reason.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.a: Double the number of members and survey again in the same way (self-selected).
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.a: Even if you increase the number of people, if they choose for themselves, the same lopsidedness arises as it is. Having more data and making the comparison fair are different things.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.b: Recommend B, which had a higher overall achievement rate, to all members and do not look further.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.b: If you decide based on the overall rate from a lopsided makeup, you throw away the information that A was higher in each course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.c: Divide the members between the two methods by drawing lots and have them practice on the same course to compare.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.c: Who uses which method is decided by chance, which reduces the lopsidedness in ability and course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.o.d: Collect and read the practice reviews of those who chose A on the hard course.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.r.d: Reviews tell the reasons, but the people who write them are lopsided too, so they are weak as comparison data.
y-m-79-02.s.s2.explain: If you assign people at random so that the two groups being compared are similar from the start, and have them practice under the same conditions, it becomes easier to see the difference in results as due to the practice method. Just increasing the number of people does not make the lopsidedness go away.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.prompt: A member said, 'B's overall achievement rate is higher, so B is better, right?' Answer this member using one or two numbers.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.hint.0: In the table, find which group's total the number the member cited is.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.hint.1: Choose one of the numbers grouped by the same course and put it in your answer.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Overall B is higher, but the makeup of courses ...
y-m-79-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear which group's achievement rate the number I cited is?
y-m-79-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you explain with the makeup of courses why the overall rate came out opposite?
y-m-79-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you mention, even in one line, the limits of self-selected data?
y-m-79-02.s.s3.model.0: Overall B looks higher, but most of those who chose B (270 people) were on the easy course, and most of A's were on the hard course (263 people). Looking within the same course, the easy course is A 93%, B 87%, and the hard course is A 73%, B 69%, so A is higher, and it is hard to say B is better from the overall rate alone.
y-m-79-02.s.s3.model.1: Difficulty affects achievement, but the two methods have different course makeups, so the overall rate is not a fair comparison. Splitting by difficulty, A is higher in both courses. However, they chose the methods themselves, so it would be more certain to divide people at random and check again.

y-m-79-03.title: A product that a '95% accurate' inspection machine called defective
y-m-79-03.topic: Conditional probability and the accuracy of a test (base rate)
y-m-79-03.goal: Confirm with numbers that when a test result says 'defective', the proportion that is really defective varies greatly with the defect rate (base rate) and the misjudgment rate, and find several cases that satisfy the conditions yourself.
y-m-79-03.material:
The following is known about a factory's automatic inspection machine.
- Defective items are 1% of all products.
- The proportion of defective items that are judged defective is 95%.
- The proportion of normal items that are wrongly judged defective is 5%.

The machine's ad says 'Accuracy 95%'. One student said, "The probability that a product the machine called defective is really defective is 95%," and worked it out like this using 10000 products.
y-m-79-03.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in the working (checking the denominator)
y-m-79-03.thinking.1: Finding several cases that satisfy the conditions
y-m-79-03.thinking.2: Saying what information is missing from the ad phrase
y-m-79-03.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: calculating percentages and ratios, and the method of setting the whole as 10000 and counting 'how many'. (You do not need to use probability formulas.) If you have already learned conditional probability, you may check the same value with the formula.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.prompt: Choose the first line in the student's working that is wrong.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.hint.0: Multiply the numbers in each line again yourself and check that they are right.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.hint.1: In the ratio on the last line, compare 'a ratio of what out of what', and whether the number you divide by is the same group as the question's 'products called defective'.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.0: If 10000 products are inspected, there are 100 defective items and 9900 normal items.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.1: Of the 100 defective items, 95% (95 items) are judged defective.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.2: Of the 9900 normal items, 5% (495 items) are also judged defective.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.3: So the products judged defective are 95 + 495 = 590.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.line.4: Of those, the really defective items are 95, so the proportion of defective judgments that are really defective is 95 ÷ 100 = 95%.
y-m-79-03.s.s1.explain: Lines 1 to 4 are right. In line 5 the 95 is right, but the number you divide by should be 590, 'all the products judged defective'. The 100 is the number of really defective items, so it doesn't match the question. 95 ÷ 590 ≈ 0.161, that is, about 16.1%.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.prompt: Consider an inspection machine with a defect rate of p%, where the proportion of normal items wrongly judged defective is q%. (The proportion of defective items judged defective stays at 95%.) Assume there are many products, and make 3 different (p, q) for which at least half (50%) of the products judged defective are really defective. p and q are integers from 1 to 10.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.hint.0: Pick one p and q, and find, out of 10000 products, the number 'judged defective that are really defective' and the number 'normal but judged defective'.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the two numbers, decide which must be larger for it to be at least half, and then change p or q one at a time.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.ok.c1: p and q are from 1 to 10.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.fail.c1: p and q must be between 1 and 10.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.fail.c2: Please enter p and q as integers.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.ok.c3: Among the defective judgments, 50% or more are really defective.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.fail.c3: Among the products judged defective, the really defective ones are less than half. Take 10000 products and compare the number of really defective judgments with the number of wrongly judged normal items.
y-m-79-03.s.s2.explain: With 10000 products, the really defective judgments number 95 × p, and the wrongly judged normal items number q × (100 − p). If the former is at least the latter, at least half of the defective judgments are really defective. (2, 1) is 190 versus 98, (5, 5) is 475 versus 475 (exactly half), and (10, 3) is 950 versus 270. (1, 1) is 95 versus 99, so it is not half.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.prompt: To a buyer who sees only the ad 'Accuracy 95%' and believes that 'if it says defective, 95% are really defective', explain what cannot be known from this number alone, and write what other information they should ask about.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write down what the two parts that make up the 590 in the working above were.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.hint.1: Find which two numbers would have to change for the sizes of those two parts to change.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Defective items are ... of the total
y-m-79-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you distinguish what the 95% is a ratio of (the proportion of defects it catches, or the proportion of judgments that are right)?
y-m-79-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say with numbers why, when the defect rate is low, there are many wrongly caught normal items?
y-m-79-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write specifically what other information is needed?
y-m-79-03.s.s3.model.0: Defective items are only 1% of the total, so normal items are overwhelmingly many, and even if just 5% of normal items are wrongly caught, that is 495, more than the 95 really defective. So even when it says defective, the proportion that is really defective is about 16%. You have to ask both the defect rate and the rate at which normal items are wrongly judged.
y-m-79-03.s.s3.model.1: You need to know whether the 95% is the proportion of defects it catches or the proportion of judgments that are right, and you also need to know the share defective items make up of the total. If the rate at which normal items are wrongly judged defective is large, there may be more normal items among those caught.

y-m-79-04.title: They say the shaved-ice shop's sales grew 30% in a month
y-m-79-04.topic: Seasonality in time-series data and year-over-year comparison
y-m-79-04.goal: Know why the growth rate over one month alone makes it hard to judge growth, and refine your judgment using a comparison with the same month last year and additional information (number of seats).
y-m-79-04.material: The shaved-ice shop's sales this June were 120만 원, and July's sales were 156만 원. The owner said, "Sales grew as much as 30% in one month, so our shop is clearly growing fast!" (Unit: 만 원. Assume both months have the same number of business days.)
y-m-79-04.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-79-04.thinking.1: Choosing the comparison base (previous month or same month last year) yourself and calculating
y-m-79-04.thinking.2: Revising your judgment with new information
y-m-79-04.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: calculating growth rates (percentages) and reading tables. In this task, the term seasonal variation is explained as roughly 'a seasonal effect that repeats every year'.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.prompt: Are the numbers above (this June 120만 원, July 156만 원) enough to say 'the shop has grown'?
y-m-79-04.s.s1.hint.0: Think about when during the year a shaved-ice shop's sales would rise and fall, and consider whether the change from June to July might occur every year.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.hint.1: Write down which two numbers you should compare to confirm 'it has grown' with the seasonal influence removed.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.a: It is enough. If sales grew as much as 30% in a month, it is clearly big growth.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.a: You read a big increase in one month as growth. For a shop affected by the seasons like shaved ice, the increase may be one that repeats every year.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.b: It is not enough. We need August's sales too before we can judge.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.b: Without waiting until August, you can change the comparison base within the data you already have.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.c: It is not enough. We also need last year's sales for the same month.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.c: This is the idea of filtering out the seasonal effect by comparing the same months.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.o.d: It is not enough. We also need the distribution of other shops' sales this year.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.r.d: Comparing with nearby shops is a useful idea too, but it does not directly help in separating whether this shop's increase is due to the season.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.explain: The increase from June to July may be due to the summer peak season. To separate growth from the seasonal effect, you need data from 'the same time', like last year's June and July.
y-m-79-04.s.s1.acc.0: Comparison with other shops is also useful information. However, to separate this shop's own seasonal effect, last year's data for the same month is more direct.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.prompt: Last year's data has arrived. Last year's June sales were 100만 원 and July's were 140만 원. Write how you would compare and calculate whether 'the shop has grown' with this data, and write what you would tell the owner as a result.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.hint.0: Pair the June sales and July sales of last year and this year, and write them in a table.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.hint.1: Find the amount of increase between the same months, and compare it side by side with the growth rate from June to July.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.placeholder: Example: Compared with the same month last year...
y-m-79-04.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you compare the same months (June with June, July with July)?
y-m-79-04.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you point out that the growth rate from June to July was similar last year too?
y-m-79-04.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Does your conclusion contradict the numbers?
y-m-79-04.s.s2.model.0: Compare with the same month last year. June grew from 100만 원 to 120만 원, up 20%, and July grew from 140만 원 to 156만 원, up about 11%. This year is also higher than last year, but the growth rate dropped, and the 30% increase from June to July was 40% last year too, so the summer effect is large.
y-m-79-04.s.s2.model.1: A comparison with the previous month mixes in the seasonal effect, so I compared last year's June-to-July growth rate (40%) with this year's growth rate (30%). This year's growth rate was lower. Sales are higher than the same months last year, so I can tell the owner that the shop has grown, but the pace has slowed.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.prompt: Newly learned information: this shop increased its number of seats by 20% over last year at the end of May this year. Reflecting this information too, what is the most fitting interpretation of the change in 'sales per seat' compared with last year? (Sales per seat = sales ÷ number of seats)
y-m-79-04.s.s3.hint.0: Divide this year's June and July sales each by 1.2, and convert them to the values for the same number of seats as last year.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.hint.1: Place the converted values next to the same months' sales last year and compare whether they are equal, bigger, or smaller.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.a: In June, sales per seat are the same as last year, and in July they dropped about 7%.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.a: You looked at the growth rate of seats together with the growth rate of sales. June is 120 ÷ 1.2 = 100, the same as last year, and July is 156 ÷ 1.2 = 130, less than last year's 140.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.b: Sales per seat increased from last year in both June and July.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.b: June sales grew 20% and seats also grew 20%. If you match the two growth rates, it is hard to say sales per seat grew.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.c: The number of seats has no effect on sales, so the earlier interpretation stands as it is.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.c: If seats increase, the customers you can serve at the same time also increase. It is hard to claim that the number of seats is unrelated to sales.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.o.d: In July, sales per seat grew about 11%, so it grew more than June.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.r.d: You mistook the sales growth rate of 11% for the growth rate of sales per seat. Divide by the fact that seats grew 20%.
y-m-79-04.s.s3.explain: Seats became 1.2 times as many, so if you divide this year's sales by 1.2 to match the number of seats to last year's basis, June is 120 ÷ 1.2 = 100 (the same as last year's 100), and July is 156 ÷ 1.2 = 130 (about 7.1% less than last year's 140). Even though sales grew, sales per seat stayed the same or fell. If the seat expansion was the reason for the sales increase, the meaning of 'growth' changes.

y-m-79-05.title: Are all the top-ranked schools small schools?
y-m-79-05.topic: Sample size and the fluctuation of the mean
y-m-79-05.goal: Explain with the number of students and the fluctuation of the mean why many small schools are at both ends of the ranking of school averages, and propose a way to change the ranking table so it is not misread.
y-m-79-05.material:
There is an article introducing each school's average on an academic achievement test (out of 100) in a region. The article wrote, "The top 3 schools by average are all small schools with 15 or fewer test-takers. Small schools have higher academic achievement."

The top 3 schools the article introduced (school, number of test-takers, average): School 가 9 students 91.2 points, School 나 15 students 89.0 points, School 다 12 students 87.5 points.
y-m-79-05.thinking.0: Judging whether the evidence is enough for the claim
y-m-79-05.thinking.1: Revising your judgment after seeing new data
y-m-79-05.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: the meaning of the mean, and the intuition that standard deviation is 'how spread out scores are from the mean'. The standard error formula (σ÷√n) is good to know beforehand but is not required.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.prompt: If you judge the article's claim that "small schools have higher academic achievement" using only the data of the 3 schools above, which is the most fitting?
y-m-79-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write down the range of schools the article picked to show.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.hint.1: Write in one line what other schools' data you would need to check the same claim.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.a: Small schools are likely to be at an advantage. The top 3 are all small schools.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.a: You can set it up as a hypothesis. But with data that looks only at the high side, you can't tell whether small schools as a whole are high.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.b: Small schools are likely to be at a disadvantage. With few students, the average is unstable.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.b: The idea that the average is unstable is important, but the direction of 'at a disadvantage' can't be known from this data alone.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.c: It is already settled. The average score is an objective number.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.c: Even if the numbers are objective, the claim can change depending on which schools were chosen to show.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.o.d: It is still hard to judge. We don't know how the averages of small schools as a whole are spread out.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.r.d: This is a judgment that weighs whether data that looks at only the top 3 supports the claim.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.explain: The article introduced only the side with the highest averages. Whether small schools as a whole are high, or whether the averages of small schools are scattered on both the high and low sides, can be known only by looking at the data of the low side and of large schools.
y-m-79-05.s.s1.acc.0: It is natural to set it up as a hypothesis. But you should not settle it, and should check with the data of the other schools.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.prompt: The office of education also released the data of the other 6 schools. The other schools (school, number of test-takers, average): School 라 11 students 64.3 points, School 마 18 students 66.0 points, School 바 120 students 78.4 points, School 사 150 students 77.9 points, School 아 210 students 78.8 points, School 자 240 students 77.5 points. Now, what is the most fitting interpretation of the article's claim and the data?
y-m-79-05.s.s2.hint.0: Line up the 9 schools in a row from the highest average, and mark small schools and large schools differently.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the length of the range where the small schools' averages lie with the length of the range where the large schools' averages lie.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.a: Keep the article's claim as it is. The top 3 are all small schools, so the effect of small schools is clear.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.a: The bottom 2 are also small schools. When you put the new data together, the statement 'the effect is clear' has weak grounds.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.b: Small schools are scattered up and down while large schools are similar, so it looks like a difference in fluctuation rather than size.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.b: You interpreted by looking at the extremes in both directions together. It connects to the explanation that the fewer the students, the more easily the average moves a lot by chance.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.c: The data contradicts itself, so no conclusion can be drawn either way, so throw the data away.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.c: It is not a contradiction but one pattern. The information itself that the small schools' averages are on both the high and low sides while the large schools are clustered is meaningful.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.o.d: Small schools are actually at a disadvantage. The bottom 2 are both small schools.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.r.d: This time you drew the opposite conclusion by looking only at the low side. You have to look together at the fact that the top 3 are small schools too.
y-m-79-05.s.s2.explain: Looking at the whole, the 5 small schools are at both ends with 91.2, 89.0, 87.5, 66.0, and 64.3 points, and the 4 large schools are clustered between 77.5 and 78.8 points. If you assume the standard deviation of individual students' scores is about 12 points, the fluctuation of the average of 9 students (standard error) is about 4.0 points, and for the average of 210 or 240 students it is about 0.8 points. This means the fewer the students, the more the average moves.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.prompt: The office of education wants to change the ranking table so it does not cause misunderstanding. Propose at least one way to change it, and write why that way reduces misunderstanding.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.hint.0: Among the information not in the current ranking table, find one that helps the reader judge whether they can trust the average.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.hint.1: Write down how reading the ranks of small schools would change if you added that information.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Write the number of students in the ranking table too, and...
y-m-79-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear what additional information my proposal gives the reader?
y-m-79-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does my proposal connect with the phenomenon of small schools crowding both ends of the ranking?
y-m-79-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you also think about the downside of my method (for example, the table becomes complicated)?
y-m-79-05.s.s3.model.0: Write the number of students in the ranking table too, and rank by grouping schools of similar size. This is because when students are few, the average changes a lot depending on a few students' scores, so it easily lands high or low by chance.
y-m-79-05.s.s3.model.1: Instead of a one-year average, use an average over the last several years, and write the margin of error next to the average. This is because a school with few students has scores that jump around from year to year, so one year's result is hard to trust.

y-m-79-06.title: Setting the price of the festival draw
y-m-79-06.topic: Expected value and designing a fair game
y-m-79-06.goal: Using expected value, make several designs for the entry fee and prizes, and explain the difference between a single result and the long-run average.
y-m-79-06.material:
At the school festival, our class is running a prize draw. There are 100 draw slips in a box, and a participant pays an entry fee of f원 and draws one slip (the calculations below use the average per slip).
- 1 first-prize slip: a gift card of P원
- 9 second-prize slips: a gift card of 2000원
- The remaining 90 slips: blank (no prize)

Our class pays the gift cards at face value. Assume there are no other costs. One student said, "I paid 1000원, got first prize, and received a gift card, so this draw is favorable to participants."
y-m-79-06.thinking.0: Spotting the error of judging by a single result
y-m-79-06.thinking.2: Explaining the difference between the average and variation
y-m-79-06.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: the meaning and calculation of expected value (the sum of prize × probability). In this task, expected value is read as 'the average payout per slip'. The law of large numbers is used only at an intuitive level.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.prompt: What is the most fitting way to evaluate the student's claim above?
y-m-79-06.s.s1.hint.0: First find what the total of the gift card amounts across all 100 slips would be.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.hint.1: Compare the 'average per slip', that total divided by 100, with the entry fee.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.a: It can't be known from a single result. We need to look at how much is received on average across all the slips.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.a: This is the idea of judging by the average of many tries rather than a single result.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.b: There is only 1 first-prize slip, so the probability is 1%, and this draw is surely unfavorable to participants.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.b: You looked only at the probability of first prize. You need to find the average including the prizes of the 9 second-prize slips.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.c: The result of trying once is the surest evidence, so the claim is right.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.c: One person's single result can be by chance. Only by playing the same game many times does the result get close to the average.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.o.d: The expected value is always equal to the amount you receive in one try, so if you calculate it, it is exactly right even for one try.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.r.d: Expected value is an idea of the average over many tries. It is not a value that must equal a single result.
y-m-79-06.s.s1.explain: A single result is greatly affected by chance. Whether this game is favorable can be known only by comparing the entry fee with the average amount received over the 100 slips (the expected value).
y-m-79-06.s.s2.prompt: Decide the first-prize gift card amount P (원) and the entry fee f (원) so that the class satisfies both of the following conditions. Make 3 different designs. (Condition 1) The average payout per slip is f or less, so our class does not lose on average. (Condition 2) The money a participant loses on average per slip (f − average payout) is 300원 or less. P is in units of 1000원 from 5000원 to 30000원, and f is in units of 100원 from 100원 to 1000원.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.hint.0: First decide on one P, find the sum of the first-prize gift card and the 9 second-prize gift cards, and divide by 100.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.hint.1: Using that average payout as the base, find the lower and upper ends of the range f can take, then pick a value in units of 100원.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The first-prize gift card keeps to the range and unit.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.fail.c1: P must be in units of 1000원 from 5000원 to 30000원.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.ok.c2: The entry fee keeps to the range and unit.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.fail.c2: f must be in units of 100원 from 100원 to 1000원.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.ok.c3: The class does not lose on average.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.fail.c3: The average payout per slip is greater than the entry fee, so the class loses on average. Compare f with the sum of the first-prize and second-prize gift card amounts divided by 100.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.ok.c4: The participant's average loss is 300원 or less.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.fail.c4: The money a participant loses on average is over 300원.
y-m-79-06.s.s2.explain: The average payout per slip is (P + 9 × 2000) ÷ 100 = P ÷ 100 + 180원. For example, if P = 10000, it is 280원, so f is from 280원 to 580원, and in units of 100원, 300, 400, and 500원 are possible. If P = 20000, the average is 380원, so f is from 400원 to 680원.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.prompt: The teacher in charge asked, "We set the price using the expected value, but if only 10 people draw slips, will our class's total profit or loss come out as planned? What if 100 people draw?" Compare the two cases and answer.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.hint.0: In the case where 10 people draw, assume that no first prize may come out or one may, and write how much the total payout would differ.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.hint.1: Thinking about how the 'average per slip' changes as the number of participants grows, compare the two cases with one sentence each.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.placeholder: Example: The more that are sold, the closer to the average...
y-m-79-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you describe the difference both when participants are few and when there are many?
y-m-79-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write in your own words 'the expected value is an average, not the result each time'?
y-m-79-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you imagine concretely a case where the class could lose when it is 10 people?
y-m-79-06.s.s3.model.0: The more that are sold, the closer the average profit or loss per slip gets to the expected value, so it ends up similar to the plan. With only 10, the first prize may come out by chance or not, so the total profit or loss can be very different from the plan.
y-m-79-06.s.s3.model.1: The expected value is the average over many tries, so even with 100 people there is no guarantee that exactly one first prize comes out, but the gap from the average shrinks. With only 10 drawing, the effect of chance is big, so the class could lose.

y-m-79-07.title: A plant height report: predicting 20 weeks later
y-m-79-07.topic: Interpreting a regression line and predicting outside the range
y-m-79-07.goal: Tell apart that a line fits well within the range of the data from that a prediction outside the range is trustworthy, and rewrite the prediction sentence with conditions attached.
y-m-79-07.material: A student measured the height of a potted plant every week. The heights (cm) from week 1 to week 6 were 5.1, 8.4, 11.3, 14.8, 18.0, 21.1 in order (the scatter plot lines up almost in a single line). The student found a line by the least squares method and wrote a report. (Calculation results: slope about 3.2, intercept about 1.9, correlation coefficient about 0.9998. Below, x is the number of weeks.)
y-m-79-07.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in the working
y-m-79-07.thinking.1: Judging what information is needed to trust a prediction
y-m-79-07.thinking.2: Rewriting a conclusion with conditions attached
y-m-79-07.prereq.0: This task is placed at the H3 (hard level) difficulty, assuming students taking the high school elective 'Practical Statistics', and it does not mean that the Ministry of Education assigns this content to a particular grade. Prerequisites: that a scatter plot and the correlation coefficient show the strength of a straight-line relationship, and interpreting the slope of a line. The line's equation has already been found, and this task does not require calculating the equation.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.prompt: Choose the line in the report that contains a wrong interpretation.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.hint.0: Mark whether the number of weeks each line talks about is inside or outside the measured range (week 1 to week 6).
y-m-79-07.s.s1.hint.1: For the line that is outside the range, think about which number of weeks the information 'the correlation coefficient is high' is about.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.0: The line for the data of weeks 1 to 6: height ≈ 3.2 × (number of weeks) + 1.9 (cm), and the correlation coefficient is about 0.9998.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.1: The correlation coefficient is very close to 1, so within the measured weeks 1 to 6, the line explains the data well.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.2: The height in week 3.5 is predicted as 3.2 × 3.5 + 1.9 = 13.1 cm.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.3: The height in week 20 is 3.2 × 20 + 1.9 = 65.9 cm, and since the correlation coefficient is high, it will be about 66 cm at week 20 too.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.line.4: The slope 3.2 means that during the measured period, the height grew by about 3.2 cm on average for each week that passed.
y-m-79-07.s.s1.explain: Line 4 is the mistake. The calculation 3.2 × 20 + 1.9 = 65.9 is right, but the high correlation coefficient means the line fit well 'within the measured weeks 1 to 6'. It is no guarantee that the plant grows at the same speed in week 20, which was not measured. Lines 1 to 3 and line 5 are right.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.prompt: To judge whether the report's prediction for week 20 is trustworthy, what information is needed? Choose everything that is needed.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.hint.0: Separate information that can tell you the height at week 20 from information that only makes the line for weeks 1 to 6 more precise.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.hint.1: For each choice, ask whether getting it would let you check if the week-20 prediction is right or wrong.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.a: The correlation coefficient recalculated to more decimal places
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.a: It only tells you more precisely how well it fits within weeks 1 to 6, and does not tell you the growth at week 20.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.b: Information that tells whether it keeps growing at the same speed after week 6 (maximum height, environment)
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.b: You chose information that directly tells how the growth outside the range might change.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.c: The result of measuring weeks 1 to 6 once more by the same method and finding the line again
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.c: Getting more data in the same range only makes the line more precise, and growth outside the range is still unknown.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.o.d: Height data of plants of the same kind actually measured after week 10
y-m-79-07.s.s2.r.d: This is data that lets you check actual values outside the range. You can compare it directly with the prediction.
y-m-79-07.s.s2.explain: A prediction outside the range needs the assumption that 'the same relationship continues in that range too'. Whether that assumption is right can be confirmed only by information such as the plant's growth characteristics or actual measurements after week 10. Handling the data of weeks 1 to 6 more precisely does not confirm this assumption.
y-m-79-07.s.s3.prompt: Rewrite line 4 of the report (the week-20 prediction) with conditions attached. Keep 66 cm as it is, but write so that it shows how this value should be read.
y-m-79-07.s.s3.hint.0: Put the range of measured weeks into the sentence as it is.
y-m-79-07.s.s3.hint.1: Write with 'if ...' what assumption must hold for it to be 66 cm.
y-m-79-07.s.s3.placeholder: Example: Within the range of weeks 1 to 6, ...
y-m-79-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the sentence I wrote make the reader take 66 cm as 'a value under an assumption' rather than 'a certain value'?
y-m-79-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write knowing the difference between a prediction inside the range (for example, week 3.5) and one outside the range?
y-m-79-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you write down at least one reason the line may not fit (for example, growth slowing or stopping)?
y-m-79-07.s.s3.model.0: Within the range of weeks 1 to 6 the line fits well, but week 20 is outside the measured range, so it is about 66 cm only if we assume it keeps growing at the same speed. In reality, growth may slow down or stop.
y-m-79-07.s.s3.model.1: The week-20 value of 66 cm is the value you get if the growth speed after week 6 stays the same. We measured only up to week 6, so we can't know what comes after, and we need to measure near week 20 directly to check.
